items.abstract:
<jats:p>Graphical user interface (GUI) agents have recently emerged as an intriguing paradigm for human-computer interaction, capable of automatically executing user instructions to operate intelligent terminal devices. 
However, when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) instructions that violate environmental constraints or exceed the current capabilities of agents, GUI agents may suffer task breakdowns or even pose security threats. Therefore, effective OOD detection for GUI agents is essential. Traditional OOD detection methods perform suboptimally in this domain due to the complex embedding space and evolving GUI environments. 
In this work, we observe that the in-distribution input semantic space of GUI agents exhibits a clustering pattern with respect to the distance from the centroid.
Based on the finding, we propose GEM, a novel method based on fitting a Gaussian mixture model over input embedding distances extracted from the GUI Agent that reflect its capability boundary. 
Evaluated on eight datasets spanning smartphones, computers, and web browsers, our method achieves an average accuracy improvement of 23.70% over the best-performing baseline while only increasing training time by 4.9% and testing time by 6.5%.
We also experimentally demonstrate that GEM can improve the step-wise success rate by 9.40% by requesting assistance from the cloud model when encountering OOD samples.
Analysis verifies the generalization ability of our method through experiments on nine different backbones.</jats:p>
title: GEM: Gaussian Embedding Modeling for Out-of-Distribution Detection in GUI Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Most modern instance-segmentation pipelines predict dense pixel masks, incurring heavy per-pixel computation. We present a compact, end-to-end trainable framework that treats instance segmentation and object detection as a unified arbitrary-shape detection problem. The key idea is to represent both a predicted parametric contour and its ground-truth as continuous Gaussian probability density fields over the image plane, and directly minimize their Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. This Gaussian Shape Embedding (GSE) converts shape matching into a smooth, differentiable loss on density fields, eliminating pixel-wise label assignments and aligning with intersection-over-union (IoU) behavior. At inference, each object is described by a short vector of shape parameters, no mask head is required. We validate GSE on standard instance-segmentation benchmark, rotated object detection and quadrilateral detection, demonstrating competitive or better results, especially at high IoU thresholds. Our results suggest GSE is a versatile foundation for detection and segmentation with diverse shape parameterizations.</jats:p>
title: Gaussian Shape Embedding: A Unified Modeling Approach for Detection and Segmentation

reference.journal-title: When integrated into a two-stage framework (RoI-Transformer with a Swin-T backbone), our loss also gives a small boost (81.01% vs 80.93% mAP reported with KFIoU). Overall, GSE matches or exceeds state-of-the-art accuracy in oriented detection
